subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation GNI stand for?
questions.explain: GNI (Gross National Income) is the total income earned by a country's people and businesses, often divided per capita to compare development.

questions.q: Which three measures are combined to calculate the Human Development Index (HDI)?
options: Life expectancy, education and income (GNI per capita)
Birth rate, death rate and migration
questions.explain: HDI combines a health measure (life expectancy), an education measure and an income measure (GNI per capita) into one value.

questions.q: Infant mortality rate is usually expressed as the number of deaths of children under one year per how many live births?
questions.explain: Infant mortality rate measures deaths of children under one year of age per 1,000 live births per year.

questions.q: Why is using GNI per capita alone a limited way to measure a country's development?
options: It is an average that can hide inequalities within a country
It cannot be measured in US dollars
It only applies to rural areas
It is always the same as HDI
questions.explain: As a mean value, GNI per capita hides the gap between rich and poor, so social development is not shown.

questions.q: Which organisation produces and publishes the Human Development Index?
questions.explain: The UNDP publishes the HDI each year to compare development across countries.

questions.q: An HDI value is given on a scale from 0 to 1. What does a value closer to 1 indicate?
questions.explain: HDI ranges from 0 to 1, and the closer the value is to 1 the more developed the country is judged to be.

questions.q: A country has a high GNI per capita but a relatively low life expectancy. What does this most likely suggest?
options: Wealth is not being converted into better health and social development for all
The country has no natural resources
The country must have the highest HDI in the world
Its birth rate must be zero
questions.explain: Economic and social indicators can conflict, showing that national wealth does not automatically improve people's wellbeing.

questions.q: Birth rate is defined as the number of live births per 1,000 of the population over what time period?
questions.explain: Birth rate is the number of live births per 1,000 people per year.

questions.q: Which of the following is a historical cause of uneven global development?
questions.explain: Colonialism exploited resources and shaped trade patterns, contributing to long-term uneven development between countries.

questions.q: In the Demographic Transition Model (DTM), which stage has both a high birth rate and a high death rate, giving a low, fluctuating population?
questions.explain: In Stage 1 high birth and high death rates roughly balance, so population stays low and fluctuating.

questions.q: What is the final stage of Rostow's modernisation (stages of growth) model?
options: The age of high mass consumption
questions.explain: Rostow's fifth and final stage is the age of high mass consumption, when a country has a developed, consumer economy.

questions.q: Frank's dependency theory explains uneven development mainly using which idea?
options: Wealth flows from poorer 'periphery' countries to richer 'core' countries
All countries pass through five identical stages
questions.explain: Dependency theory argues rich core countries keep poorer periphery countries dependent, draining their wealth and resources.

questions.q: A landlocked country with mountainous terrain struggles to develop. Which type of cause of uneven development does this best illustrate?
questions.explain: Being landlocked with difficult terrain is a physical factor that raises trade costs and can slow development.

questions.q: Which of the following is a consequence, rather than a cause, of uneven development?
options: International migration of people seeking work
questions.explain: People often migrate from poorer to richer areas or countries as a result of the gap in wealth and opportunity.

questions.q: An emerging country such as India belongs to which well-known group of rapidly growing economies?
questions.explain: BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa) is a grouping of major emerging economies.

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage for an emerging country when a transnational corporation (TNC) invests there?
options: It creates jobs and can bring new skills and technology
All profits stay entirely within the host country
It reduces the country's exports to zero
It removes the need for any workers
questions.explain: TNC investment can create employment, transfer skills and technology, and boost the local economy.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common disadvantage of TNCs operating in an emerging country?
options: Much of the profit is sent back to the company's home country
They always pay the highest wages in the world
They guarantee equal wealth for everyone
questions.explain: Profits are often repatriated to the TNC's headquarters, so the host country keeps only part of the wealth created.

questions.q: A richer country funds a project to build schools and train teachers in a developing country over many years. Which type of aid is this?
questions.explain: Long-term development aid supports lasting improvements such as education, health and infrastructure over time.

questions.q: How does Fairtrade aim to help producers in developing and emerging countries?
options: By guaranteeing them a fair, minimum price for their goods
By removing all trade between countries
By giving producers no payment until goods are sold
By banning the export of crops
questions.explain: Fairtrade guarantees producers a minimum price and a premium, giving them a more secure and fair income.

questions.q: A charity introduces simple, low-cost water pumps that local people can repair themselves. This is an example of what approach to development?
questions.explain: Intermediate or appropriate technology is affordable, small-scale and suited to local skills and resources, making it sustainable.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Geography B (1GB0) specification; Global Development
